newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.

text.p: ROTHWELLS CONVICTIONS WELCOMED

The former head of the National Companies and Securities Commission Henry Bosch says the convictions in the Rothwells conspiracy trial will show foreigners that Australian justice works, at least sometimes.
Former Rothwells director Peter Lucas and auditor Louis Carter have been convicted of conspiring to conceal the true financial position of the bank before its collapse in 1988.
Bosch, who headed the NCSC during the 1980's, says the outcome of the case will enhance Australia's international reputation as a place to invest.
But he says the time taken to bring the offenders to justice is a black mark against Australia's legal system.
ClAIMS THAT WORKCOVER DEBT TO RISE
The New South Wales government says the opposition has added A$36 million to the Workcover debt by insisting on workers' compensation amendments, moved in Parliament last night.
The Workcover debt is already running at more than A$300 million and Industrial Relations Minister Jeff Shaw says the amendments will be costly.

But he has welcomed the return of no-fault journey claims after the government won enough support from the cross-benches to ensure that workers injured on the way to or from their jobs will be entitled to compensation.
The opposition says its amendments are a win for employers, with the excess paid by employers to an injured employee being restricted to A$500, instead of two weeks' salary.
AIR FORCE RECRUITS FOREIGN PILOTS
The Air Force has confirmed it's recruiting foreign pilots to replace Australian officers who are being lured away by commercial airlines.
The RAAF has been hiring pilots from Canada, the United States and the United Kingdom and other countries to ensure air force planes can stay in the air.
A Defence Department spokesman says he's unaware of any move to rapidly increase foreign recuitments but overseas-trained pilots have long been interested in joining the RAAF.
FEWER LOANS THROUGH CREDIT UNIONS
Australia's credit unions saw demand for loans dip in the September quarter, in the wake of strong competition, particularly from the banks.
The credit union watchdog, the Australian Financial Institutions Commission, says loans in the quarter rose 1.4 percent, to A$12.4 billion.
That compares with growth rates of more than two percent in the previous four quarters. However credit union deposits increased by four percent to A$14.1.
MINE WORKERS TO BE REMEMBERED
A memorial service will be held in Newcastle today for the four miners killed at the Gretley Colliery earlier this month.
Mark Kaiser, John Hunter, Damon Murray and Edward Batterham, died when the section of tunnel they were working in flooded with water.

Attending today's service at the sacred heart cathedral in Hamilton will be Premier Bob Carr, NSW Governor Gordon Samuels, Federal Resources Minister, Warwick Parer, and his State counterpart, Bob Martin.
The Miners Union says it expects around one thousand people to attend the service.
TASMANIA STUDIES AFL BENEFITS
A Federal Government inquiry into Tasmania's economy is to look at the economic advantages of the state being involved in the Australian Football League.
Premier Tony Rundle says he's asked the chairman of the inquiry, Peter Nixon, to look into the benefits or otherwise of Tasmania joining the competition.

Mr Rundle says while the Government's ability to contribute financially to Tasmania joining the AFL is limited, he's supporting efforts by the Tasmanian Football League's chief commissioner, Michael Kent, to bring it about.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
